newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wins major court victory against Staples.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wins major court victory against Staples.

text.p: The proposed $4 billion merger between office superstore chains Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. was put into doubt Monday when a federal judge granted government trustbusters a crucial preliminary injunction, Federal Trade Commission lawyers said.
The FTC had argued that the combined chains would have the power to raise consumer prices.

Wall Street analysts speculated that the companies would soon call off the merger after the latest blow to the 10-month-old proposed deal. Analysts and traders said the two companies were unlikely to appeal the decision by U.S. District Judge Thomas Hogan.
"The deal is dead. The companies will go their own ways and pursue their own strategies," said Mark Mandel of The Chicago Corp.

A preliminary injunction prevents the merger until the case works its way through the courts, which could take a year or more. Under the law, the next step is for the FTC to conduct a months-long administrative trial on the merits of the merger.
Staples attorney Don Kemps said he was "stunned" by Hogan's ruling. He said Staples would decide within four days whether to appeal, then quickly left the court building.

Staples President Thomas Stemberg said last month that if Hogan granted the preliminary injunction, he would give up the costly court fight -- which has cost the two firms more than $12 million -- and the merger would be dead.
Office Depot said in a statement it was disappointed in the judge's decision.

"The boards of directors of both Office Depot and Staples still need to review the judge's ruling and a decision by the boards on whether or not to appeal will be made in the next few days," Office Depot said.
It said its core management team remains in place and that Office Depot would immediately begin to aggressively recruit people for open positions.
